exam: What is the first step if a patient develops vomiting within 24 h of cisplatin? — Give anti‑emetics and ensure hydration.
How would you differentiate platinum‑induced neuropathy from diabetic neuropathy in a patient with HIV? — Look for acute onset, stocking‑glove distribution, and absence of glycaemic control issues.
A patient on cisplatin develops a sudden rise in serum creatinine. What is the immediate management? — Stop the drug, start aggressive hydration, and consider switching to carboplatin.
Why is carboplatin preferred in patients with pre‑existing renal impairment? — It has a longer half‑life and less nephrotoxicity.
During a ward round, a patient on oxaliplatin reports tinnitus. What should you do? — Assess hearing, document, and consider dose reduction or discontinuation.
If a patient cannot afford routine blood tests, what bedside monitoring can you rely on for nephrotoxicity? — Monitor urine output and look for oliguria.
ai.title: Platinum Compounds in Oncology
ai.subject: Pharmacology
ai.summary: Platinum agents are alkylating chemotherapeutics that cross‑link DNA, blocking tumour cell replication. Their use in low‑resource settings hinges on recognising toxicity, managing side effects, and adapting monitoring when laboratory tests are limited.

b: Cisplatin – first‑line for testicular, ovarian, bladder, head and neck cancers
Carboplatin – used where renal toxicity is a concern
Oxaliplatin – part of FOLFOX for colorectal cancer
sections.p: Platinum compounds are metal‑based drugs that form covalent bonds with DNA, creating cross‑links that prevent replication. Diagnosis of exposure is clinical; laboratory confirmation is rarely required.

b: Grade 1–2: mild, manageable with supportive care
sections.p: Toxicity is graded by the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE). Grade 3–4 events (e.g., nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity) necessitate dose reduction or discontinuation.

t.b: Assess renal function; rise >1.5× baseline indicates nephrotoxicity

sections.p: The primary causes of toxicity are drug properties and patient factors common in low‑resource settings.

t.b: Oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/h) indicates acute kidney injury

b: Chronic: numbness in feet, tinnitus, decreased urine output
sections.p: Patients may develop nausea, vomiting, fever, myalgia, and, with repeated doses, sensorineural hearing loss, peripheral neuropathy, and nephrotoxicity.

b: Audiometry if available; otherwise ask about hearing changes
sections.p: Baseline and periodic monitoring are essential, but many tests may be unavailable. Use clinical judgement and simple bedside tools.

t.b: Detect myelosuppression; low platelets can cause bleeding

b: Severe paresthesia with loss of reflexes
sections.p: Certain signs warrant urgent action: severe renal failure, profound neurotoxicity, uncontrolled bleeding, or anaphylaxis.

b: Avoid NSAIDs and other nephrotoxic agents
sections.p: Treat the underlying toxicity, provide supportive care, and adjust chemotherapy dosing. Avoid drugs that worsen the same organ system.

b: Educate on hydration and early symptom reporting
sections.p: Regular monitoring of renal function, electrolytes, and neuro‑sensory status is mandatory. Patient education on reporting symptoms early is key.
Other causes of nausea, vomiting, and neuropathy can mimic platinum toxicity.

b: Audiometry may not be available; rely on patient history
sections.p: Some laboratory values may be falsely normal or misleading in resource‑limited settings.

whenToSeekHelp: Loss of consciousness or severe neurotoxicity
